name: Standard Route / South Side

waypoints.name: Hairpin Turn Pullout, SR-20
waypoints.note: Large roadside pullout on the outside of the SR-20 hairpin switchback (~MP 163); no permit needed, boot path drops south into the trees toward Early Winters Creek.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the large roadside pullout at the hairpin turn near Milepost 163, just below Washington Pass. No permit or pass is needed to park there. This is the North Cascades Highway, so the drive only exists once SR-20 opens for the season — it usually reopens in April or early May and closes again in late November or early December. From the pullout the boot path drops south off the shoulder into the trees and fords Early Winters Creek directly across from the parking area; there is no maintained trail or trail number above the highway.

waypoints.name: Early Winters Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Early Winters Creek on the climbers' path just past the pullout; can run high and fast with June snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' trail gains the Kangaroo Ridge crest here after ~1,500 ft of climbing through trees and the lower gully; route-finding is easy below but the path is faint near the top.

waypoints.name: Snow-filled gully below Big Kangaroo
waypoints.note: Parallel gullies angling up the west face beneath Big Kangaroo hold snow well into July; ice axe recommended for the ascending traverse.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Ridge basin
waypoints.note: Talus basin below Big Kangaroo and Mushroom Tower where the standard route splits off toward Mushroom Tower's south side; class 3 scrambling begins here.

waypoints.name: Base of South Side route
waypoints.note: Roped low-5th-class climbing starts here; rack light with a few small cams for the step-across move higher up.

waypoints.name: Step-across move to summit block
waypoints.note: Exposed step-across move gains the blocky, semi-detached summit block; the route's crux and essentially unprotected.

waypoints.name: Mushroom Tower summit
waypoints.note: Small blocky summit; rappel begins from a fixed anchor of two old 1/4-inch bolts to reverse the ascent route.

approach: From the large pullout on the inside of the Hairpin Turn on SR-20 (~Milepost 163, roughly 5,150 ft, just below Washington Pass), drop off the highway shoulder and ford Early Winters Creek directly across from the parking area — expect wet feet in early-season high water; by mid-to-late summer it braids down to an easy rock-hop. From the far bank, head straight up into timber on climber's-left of the obvious drainage gully that falls from Kangaroo Ridge; a boot-path stays in the trees rather than fighting brush in the gully bottom itself. As the trees thin, keep to the left (south) side of the gully and follow it onto the ridge crest above, mixing dirt/heather benches with short bouts of easy Class 2-3 scrambling. This is the shared approach line for all of the Kangaroo Ridge towers (Big Kangaroo, Half Moon, Mushroom Tower) and packs about 3,000 ft of gain into well under 2 miles, so it is steep and sustained the whole way — plan on 2.5-4 hours up for a party unfamiliar with it. Where the ridge steepens below the final rock tiers, traverse left (west) beneath the base of the wall and climb a band of steep snow (a snowfinger that lingers on this shaded aspect well into summer) to reach the notch/base directly under Mushroom Tower's summit block; an ice axe is standard here and crampons are worth carrying in early season, per a June trip report that found this stretch snow-covered enough to boot steps the whole way. There is no reliable water above the initial creek ford, so treat that crossing as your last easy fill-up. There is no maintained trail or trail number above the highway — it is entirely a climber's boot-path, and route-finding is straightforward in clear weather (aim for the mushroom-capped tower on the skyline) but unforgiving in fog or whiteout given the mix of gully, timber, and traverse terrain.
descent_text: The route tops out with a short, exposed step/traverse across a gap just below the true summit block, which trip reports flag as the technical crux and note it can be wet or verglassed when snow is still sitting on top of the tower. Descent from the summit is a single rappel — well under one rope length — off a fixed anchor of two old 1/4-inch bolts placed by Fred Beckey's party during the June 1942 first ascent of the Kangaroo Ridge towers; a 2010 trip report documented these as already 68 years old at that time, meaning the hardware standing today is original-vintage 1940s-era bolts, not a modern re-bolt. Inspect it closely before trusting it and back it up (or extend/replace) if you're carrying the means to do so. A standard doubled rope (e.g., a 60m rope folded to give 30m per strand, or even a doubled 30m rope) reaches with room to spare; a single-strand rappel on a 30m+ rope would also work if that suits your retrieval plan. The rappel lands on south-side scramble terrain; from there, downclimb/scramble back to the notch and reverse the ascent traverse and snowfinger to the head of the approach gully. Descend the same climber's-left line used on the way up — the gully commonly holds snow late into the season and can be partially glissaded, which speeds the descent but carries runout and rockfall-channel exposure once the snow softens in the afternoon sun, so timing matters. Continue down through timber to Early Winters Creek, re-ford, and you're back at the Hairpin Turn pullout. This is not a walk-off: even though the technical climbing is short (2 pitches), the exposed summit step and the fixed-anchor rappel mean a rope, harness, and rappel device are mandatory gear, not optional. Round-trip car-to-car time for a party familiar with the route runs roughly 6-8 hours.

pitch_detail.notes: From the notch below the tower (reached via the snowfinger traverse), climb low-fifth-class blocky granite up the south side, picking the path of least resistance on generally solid but sometimes lichen-dusted rock. Gear placements in the horizontal breaks are straightforward and this pitch is mostly a rope-up formality over what would otherwise be Class 4 scrambling.

The pitch is short but ends at the route's namesake feature: an exposed step-across a gap to gain the overhanging, mushroom-capped summit block, which trip reports flag as the technical crux and note can feel harder when wet or still verglassed from lingering snow. Top out directly at the two original 1/4-inch bolts placed by Fred and Helmy Beckey's party on the 1942 first ascent of the Kangaroo Ridge towers, used today as the descent rap anchor.
